chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan, from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

When a man says, 'Upon me is the walking to the House of Allah,' while he is in Ihram for a Hajj, or 'Upon me is such and such an offering,' it is not valid (as a vow) until he says, 'For the sake of Allah, upon me is the walking to His House,' or he says, 'For the sake of Allah, upon me is that I should enter Ihram for a Hajj,' or he says, 'For the sake of Allah, upon me is such and such an offering, if I do not do such and such.'

key_terms.إِحْرَام: Ihram: The state of ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah
key_terms.لِلَّهِ: Lillahi: For the sake of Allah; the essential phrase validating the vow
key_terms.نَذْر: Nadhr: A vow or pledge to perform an act of worship
key_terms.هَدْي: Hady: An animal offering sacrificed during Hajj

ai.seo_question: What is the correct verbal formula for a valid vow (nadhr) in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi emphasizes the precise linguistic formulation required for a vow (nadhr) to be legally binding, distinguishing between a simple self-imposed obligation and a religious vow dedicated to Allah. It highlights the Shia scholarly focus on the explicit invocation of 'For the sake of Allah' (lillahi) as the essential condition that transforms a personal intention into a binding religious duty, ensuring the vow is an act of worship rather than mere resolve.
